people.name: Augustine of Hippo
people.summary: North African rhetorician turned bishop, the most influential Latin theologian: the Confessions (c. 397-400), On the Trinity, and the City of God (413-426), written in answer to the sack of Rome. He fought Donatists, Manichaeans and Pelagians and died during the Vandal siege of Hippo.
people.detail: His letters, including the Divjak letters discovered in 1975, show a bishop handling slave traders, land disputes and imperial officials. His doctrine of grace and original sin shaped western Christianity, and his political theology detached the church's destiny from Rome's.
people.death: fever during the Vandal siege of Hippo, 28 August 430
scholarship: Brown, Augustine of Hippo (1967, rev. 2000)

people.name: Jerome
people.summary: Dalmatian-born scholar and ascetic, translator of most of the Latin Vulgate Bible, who lived at Bethlehem from 386. His letters on the Rhine crossing (Ep. 123) and the sack of Rome (Ep. 127, 128) are among the most quoted responses to the western catastrophe.
scholarship: Kelly, Jerome (1975)

people.name: John Chrysostom
people.summary: Antiochene preacher of genius, archbishop of Constantinople from 398, whose reforming zeal and sermons against the rich and the court earned the enmity of the empress Eudoxia and Theophilus of Alexandria. Deposed at the Synod of the Oak and exiled in 404, he died on a forced march.
people.death: exhaustion during forced march at Comana Pontica, 14 September 407

sources.w: Dialogue on the Life of John Chrysostom

scholarship: Kelly, Golden Mouth (1995)

people.name: Cyril of Alexandria
people.summary: Combative patriarch who expelled Alexandria's Jews and Novatians, was implicated by association in the murder of Hypatia, and engineered the condemnation of Nestorius at Ephesus in 431. His Christology, emphasising the one nature of the incarnate Word, was claimed by both Chalcedonians and their opponents.
scholarship: McGuckin, St Cyril of Alexandria (1994)

people.name: Nestorius
people.summary: Antiochene monk made archbishop of Constantinople in 428, who objected to calling Mary Theotokos ('God-bearer'), preferring Christotokos. Condemned at Ephesus in 431 and exiled to Egypt, he wrote a defence, the Book of Heracleides, surviving in Syriac. The Church of the East venerates him.

people.name: Pope Leo I
people.summary: Bishop of Rome whose Tome (449) defined the two natures of Christ and was acclaimed at Chalcedon ('Peter has spoken through Leo'). He led the embassy that met Attila in 452 and negotiated with Gaiseric in 455. He articulated the theory of papal primacy as the heir of Peter.
scholarship: Wessel, Leo the Great and the Spiritual Rebuilding of a Universal Rome (2008)

people.name: Dioscorus of Alexandria
people.summary: Cyril's successor, who presided over the 'Robber Synod' of Ephesus in 449, rehabilitating Eutyches and deposing Flavian. Deposed at Chalcedon in 451 (formally for contumacy) and exiled to Gangra. Venerated as a saint by the Coptic Church.

people.name: Eutyches
people.summary: Elderly archimandrite and godfather of the eunuch Chrysaphius, who taught that after the union Christ had only one nature, his humanity absorbed in his divinity. Condemned by Flavian in 448, rehabilitated in 449, condemned again at Chalcedon. Both Chalcedonians and miaphysites rejected his views.

people.name: Severus of Antioch
people.summary: Leading anti-Chalcedonian theologian, patriarch of Antioch under Anastasius, deposed by Justin I in 518. From exile in Egypt he shaped miaphysite doctrine; his huge corpus survives mainly in Syriac. Justinian condemned him in 536.

people.name: Pope Vigilius
people.summary: Roman deacon installed as pope by Belisarius and Antonina in 537 after the deposition of Silverius, allegedly with a secret promise to Theodora to reject Chalcedon. Detained in Constantinople from 547, he vacillated over the Three Chapters, fled to sanctuary, and finally accepted the council of 553.
people.death: at Syracuse on his way back to Rome, 7 June 555

people.name: Gregory the Great
people.summary: Aristocratic urban prefect turned monk and pope, who governed Rome amid Lombard war and plague, negotiated with Agilulf, sent Augustine to the English (597), and wrote the Pastoral Rule, the Moralia on Job and the Dialogues. His Register of 854 letters is a unique window on late sixth-century Italy and the papal estates.
scholarship: Markus, Gregory the Great and His World (1997)

people.name: Sergius I of Constantinople
people.summary: Syrian-born patriarch, Heraclius's closest collaborator: he crowned him, lent church treasure for the Persian war, led the defence of Constantinople in 626 with icon processions, and devised Monoenergism and the Ecthesis. Condemned posthumously as a heretic in 681.

people.name: Sophronius of Jerusalem
people.summary: Damascene monk and travelling companion of John Moschus, leading opponent of Monoenergism, elected patriarch of Jerusalem in 634. His Christmas sermon of 634 laments that Christians could not reach Bethlehem because of the 'Saracens'. He surrendered the city to Umar.
scholarship: Booth, Crisis of Empire (2014)

people.name: Cyrus of Alexandria
people.summary: Heraclius's patriarch and governor of Egypt, who imposed the Monoenergist union of 633 and persecuted the Coptic church. Probably the al-Muqawqis of Arab tradition, he negotiated the surrender of Babylon and the Treaty of Alexandria with Amr ibn al-As in 641.

sources.a: History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria

people.name: Procopius of Caesarea
people.summary: The great historian of Justinian's age. Present at Dara, in Africa and in Italy with Belisarius, he wrote the Wars (8 books), the Buildings (a panegyric of Justinian's construction), and the Secret History (Anekdota), a savage, unpublished attack on Justinian, Theodora, Belisarius and Antonina.
people.detail: A classicising historian modelled on Thucydides and Herodotus, he is indispensable for military history but must be read with attention to his biases: hero-worship and disillusion with Belisarius, hostility to John the Cappadocian, and conflicting views of Justinian across his works. Kaldellis reads him as a covert critic of autocracy; Cameron as a more conventional mind. Whether he is the Procopius who was urban prefect in 562 is uncertain.
scholarship: Cameron, Procopius and the Sixth Century (1985)
Kaldellis, Procopius of Caesarea (2004)
Greatrex, 'Perceptions of Procopius in recent scholarship', Histos 8 (2014)

people.name: Zosimus
people.summary: Pagan historian writing in Constantinople around 500, whose New History in six books blames Rome's decline on the abandonment of the traditional gods. For 395-410 he follows Eunapius and then Olympiodorus closely, making him the main narrative source for Stilicho and Alaric. His text breaks off in summer 410, just before the sack.
scholarship: Paschoud (ed.), Zosime: Histoire nouvelle (1971-89)

people.name: Olympiodorus of Thebes
people.summary: Egyptian poet and diplomat who travelled with a pet parrot, went on an embassy to the Huns, and wrote a history of the West from 407 to 425 in 22 books, surviving only in Photius's summary and through Zosimus, Sozomen and Philostorgius. It is the best-informed source for the fall of Stilicho, the sack of Rome and Galla Placidia.
scholarship: Blockley, The Fragmentary Classicising Historians of the Later Roman Empire (1981-83)

people.name: Priscus of Panium

roles.t: Member of the embassy to Attila

people.summary: Thracian rhetor and diplomat, eyewitness of Attila's court in 449, whose classicising history (covering c. 434-474) survives only in fragments in the tenth-century Excerpta de legationibus and in Jordanes and Evagrius. His Hunnic material is unique and vivid but literary, including the famous debate with a Greek who had become a Hun.
scholarship: Blockley, The Fragmentary Classicising Historians (1981-83)
Given (trans.), The Fragmentary History of Priscus (2014)

people.name: Agathias
people.summary: Poet and lawyer from Myrina who continued Procopius with a history of 552-559 in five books: Narses's Italian campaigns, the Lazic war, the Kutrigur invasion and Belisarius's last victory, with a digression on Persian customs drawn from royal annals via the interpreter Sergius. He also compiled the Cycle, an anthology of epigrams.
scholarship: Cameron, Agathias (1970)

people.name: Theophylact Simocatta
people.summary: Egyptian-born official under Heraclius, last of the classicising historians, whose History in eight books covers Maurice's reign (582-602) in a famously florid style. Indispensable for the Persian war of 572-591, the restoration of Khosrow II and the Balkan campaigns, it ends with Phocas's coup.
scholarship: Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and his Historian (1988)
Whitby & Whitby (trans.), The History of Theophylact Simocatta (1986)

people.name: Jordanes

roles.t: Notarius of the magister militum Gunthigis

people.summary: Latin-speaking official of Gothic descent in Constantinople who in 551 wrote the Romana and the Getica, a summary of Cassiodorus's lost Gothic History. The Getica's account of Gothic origins in 'Scandza', the Catalaunian Plains and Attila's death is central to Gothic history but heavily debated.
scholarship: Goffart, The Narrators of Barbarian History (1988)
Christensen, Cassiodorus, Jordanes and the History of the Goths (2002)

people.name: Orosius
people.summary: Spanish priest from Bracara who joined Augustine in Africa and wrote the Seven Books of History against the Pagans (416-417), a providential universal history and a contemporary source for the Gothic wars and the sack of 410.

people.name: Sidonius Apollinaris
people.summary: Gallo-Roman aristocrat, poet and letter-writer, son-in-law of Avitus, who delivered panegyrics on three emperors (Avitus, Majorian, Anthemius), became urban prefect, and as bishop of Clermont led its resistance to Euric. His letters are the best portrait of Gallic aristocratic society as Roman rule ended.
scholarship: Harries, Sidonius Apollinaris and the Fall of Rome (1994)

people.name: Boethius
people.summary: Roman senator and philosopher who translated and commented on Aristotle's logic, wrote on music, arithmetic and theology, and served Theodoric as magister officiorum. Convicted of treason, he wrote the Consolation of Philosophy in prison before his execution; it became one of the most read books of the Middle Ages.
scholarship: Chadwick, Boethius: The Consolations of Music, Logic, Theology and Philosophy (1981)

people.name: Cassiodorus
people.summary: Calabrian senator who served the Ostrogothic kings for thirty years, writing their official letters (Variae), a Chronicle and a lost Gothic History used by Jordanes. After years in Constantinople he founded the monastery of Vivarium, where his Institutiones laid out a programme for preserving sacred and secular learning.
people.death: natural causes at Vivarium, c. 585, aged about 100
scholarship: O'Donnell, Cassiodorus (1979)

people.name: Claudian

roles.t: Court poet of Honorius and Stilicho

people.summary: Alexandrian Greek who became the last great classical Latin poet, writing panegyrics for Stilicho and Honorius and invectives against Rufinus and Eutropius. His poems are propaganda but our main contemporary source for western politics 395-404.
scholarship: Cameron, Claudian: Poetry and Propaganda at the Court of Honorius (1970)

people.name: John Malalas
people.summary: Antiochene official whose Chronographia in 18 books, from Adam to 563, written in a Greek closer to the spoken language, is the first surviving Byzantine world chronicle. Uncritical for earlier periods but valuable for sixth-century Antioch and Constantinople, including Nika, the Antioch earthquake and the Academy edict.
scholarship: Jeffreys, Jeffreys & Scott (trans.), The Chronicle of John Malalas (1986)

people.name: Gregory of Tours
people.summary: Gallo-Roman aristocrat and bishop of Tours whose Ten Books of Histories are the principal source for Clovis and the Merovingian Franks, as well as hagiographies of Martin and other saints. His account of Clovis's conversion and wars is shaped by his theological purposes.
scholarship: Heinzelmann, Gregory of Tours: History and Society in the Sixth Century (2001)
Goffart, The Narrators of Barbarian History (1988)

people.name: Menander Protector
people.summary: Constantinopolitan who, after a dissolute youth, joined the palace guard and wrote a continuation of Agathias covering 558-582 under Maurice's patronage. Fragments preserved in the Excerpta de legationibus contain the full terms of the 562 treaty with Persia and accounts of embassies to the Avars and Turks.
scholarship: Blockley (ed.), The History of Menander the Guardsman (1985)

people.name: Anthemius of Tralles
people.summary: Mathematician and engineer from Tralles, co-designer of Hagia Sophia with Isidore of Miletus. He wrote on burning mirrors and conic sections, and Agathias tells that he frightened a neighbour with a simulated earthquake made with steam-driven leather tubes.

people.name: Isidore of Miletus
people.summary: Geometer and engineer who completed Hagia Sophia with Anthemius of Tralles and edited Archimedes' works, an edition that helped them survive. His nephew Isidore the Younger rebuilt the dome after 558.

people.name: George of Pisidia

roles.t: Deacon and skeuophylax of Hagia Sophia

people.summary: Court poet of Heraclius and Patriarch Sergius, whose iambic poems (Expeditio Persica on the 622 campaign, Bellum Avaricum on the 626 siege, Heraclias on the victory) are the main contemporary literary sources for the Persian war, used by Theophanes.
scholarship: Whitby, 'George of Pisidia's presentation of the emperor Heraclius', in Dabrowa (ed.), The Roman and Byzantine Army in the East (1994)

people.name: Evagrius Scholasticus

roles.t: Lawyer, adviser to the patriarch of Antioch

people.summary: Lawyer from Epiphania in Syria whose Ecclesiastical History (431-594) is a key Chalcedonian source for the period. He survived the plague as a child and lost wife, children and grandchildren to its later waves, which he describes vividly.
scholarship: Whitby (trans.), The Ecclesiastical History of Evagrius Scholasticus (2000)

people.name: Hydatius
people.summary: Bishop in Gallaecia whose chronicle (379-468) is the main source for fifth-century Spain under Sueves, Vandals and Goths, written in an apocalyptic mood from a province abandoned by imperial power. He went on an embassy to Aetius in 431.
scholarship: Burgess (ed.), The Chronicle of Hydatius (1993)

people.name: Victor of Vita
people.summary: African cleric who around 484-489 wrote the History of the Vandal Persecution, a passionate account of Arian persecution of the Nicene church under Gaiseric and Huneric, and the source of the figure of 80,000 Vandals crossing in 429.
scholarship: Moorhead (trans.), Victor of Vita: History of the Vandal Persecution (1992)

people.name: Muhammad

roles.t: Prophet and leader of the community at Medina

people.summary: Meccan merchant and prophet of Islam, who migrated to Medina in 622, unified much of Arabia by 630, and sent the first expeditions against Roman Syria (Mu'ta, 629; Tabuk, 630). The armies of his successors overran Syria, Egypt and Persia within a decade of his death.
scholarship: Donner, Muhammad and the Believers (2010)
Hoyland, Seeing Islam as Others Saw It (1997)

people.name: Abu Bakr
people.summary: Muhammad's companion and father-in-law, first caliph, who crushed the Ridda revolts and launched the invasions of Iraq and Syria, sending Khalid ibn al-Walid across the desert to Syria in 634.

people.name: Umar ibn al-Khattab
people.summary: Second caliph, under whom the Arabs conquered Syria (Yarmuk 636), Iraq (Qadisiyya c. 636), Jerusalem, Mesopotamia and Egypt. He received Jerusalem's surrender in person, created the diwan register of pensions, and fixed the Hijra calendar. Murdered in 644 by a Persian slave.
people.death: stabbed in the mosque at Medina, November 644

people.name: Khalid ibn al-Walid

roles.t: Commander in the Ridda wars and Iraq

people.summary: 'The Sword of God': Meccan cavalry commander who fought against Muhammad at Uhud, converted in 629, saved the army at Mu'ta, crushed the Ridda, campaigned in Iraq, crossed the desert to Syria in 634 and was a leading commander at Ajnadayn, Damascus and the Yarmuk. Umar removed him from supreme command.
scholarship: Donner, The Early Islamic Conquests (1981)

people.name: Amr ibn al-As
people.summary: Meccan Qurashi commander who had traded in Egypt before Islam, led the army of Palestine (634-639), invaded Egypt in December 639, won at Heliopolis, took Babylon and negotiated the Treaty of Alexandria. He founded Fustat and later supported Mu'awiya.

people.name: Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah
people.fullName: Amir ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Jarrah
people.summary: Early companion of Muhammad, appointed by Umar to replace Khalid as supreme commander in Syria; overall commander at the Yarmuk and in the conquest of Damascus, Emesa, Antioch and Jerusalem. He died in the plague of Amwas.
